utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-R77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I say at the outset that we're making every effort to complete the case today, and I ask all parties to take that into consideration. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to call Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your full name is Igor Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, let's come straight to the point. You were sitting in court yesterday when a tape recording was played of a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you one of the parties to that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall it now?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where were you when that telephone conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the street in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So it follows, does it, that you were speaking on a mobile phone?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During the course of that conversation, the other party to the telephone call talked to you about a programme?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you understand what he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your attitude to that telephone conversation generally?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a question of interpretation. I mean, in slang language we used to use this word as an event or gathering or -- I mean, in terms of, "What is the programme for tonight?" that kind of thing. In this particular moment and this case, I was probably -- my understanding was probably that it was related to some kind of trial proceedings or some witness protection programme or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, if, as you say, you had no idea what the programme referred to, why in the world would you say that it was sometime in November? What kind of programme is going on sometime in November?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ryneveld, let me explain it to you. The term "programme" -- as I said, in our language, slang -- we used to use on a daily basis, means to me that if I'm speaking with friends. That's another meaning, as I just explained. On this particular occasion, my understanding was that this programme means an event, means some kind of procedures, some kind of, as I said, a witness protection programme, because I remember that we have discussed that on many occasions, all the colleagues in this joinder case, this issue. Because, you know, to have a proper defence in this particular case, it is not enough to bring Serb witnesses here. Our defence strategy was based on the fact that we would need to have witnesses from the other nationalities and, well, it's a very sensitive issue. Most of them always asked, "What kind of protection will we have in The Hague? What is the procedure? What is the travel arrangements?" and many other things. So probably my understanding was that it was related to something on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you did discuss this file with Mr. Avramovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: We always discuss. Not only me and Avramovic, but me and my learned colleagues Pisarevic, Brashich, and the others. I mean, it's the process. We are all discussing general issues of the law, issues of proceedings and including relations with witnesses and all these things. I mean, it's a joinder case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you didn't say, "I don't know what programme you're talking about." When he said, "When did that programme with Bane start," your answer is, "Toward the end of the year."

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: My belief is that it was related to some kind of process. I didn't know in which capacity this person is making some relations with my colleague or who -- even I don't know him in person. And as you may take a short look on the second page of your transcript, you'll see that there is a small pause, so it was -- in fact, it was a little bit strange to me to give the answer like that. But don't forget, Mr. Ryneveld, that I was in Belgrade. It was, I think, early in the evening. The air strike alert was just to be announced. It was a bombing operation against Yugoslavia. I was heading to the other part of town to be, you know -- across the bridge, et cetera. When I came from the Hague after the last Status Conference at the end of April 29th, then we set a trial date for 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: The immense extraordinary efforts for us to prepare the case, to arrange all necessary things, not to mention travels and all these things, under these circumstances, it was so, so complicated. There was no electricity. Our work in our offices was practically stopped, you know, in many period of days. So probably I was not -- I wasn't so focussed on this kind of word. As you can also see in this transcript, there is a few things which is unintelligible or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a street, it's noise, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Although, sir, in fairness, not in the portion with you and Daki; this is in the second part of the transcript, Bane and Daki, that it is unintelligible. Your --

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can just take a look on the first page. It says.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't see a lot of unintelligible aspects to the part of the conversation attributed to you, sir, but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe you should not be so ironic, my dear friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm just looking, and I don't see any. Well, there's one, "Igor: (Unintelligible)," near the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's minor, I would say. It's not so important a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I only have a couple more questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I understand your position, you were busy, you had lots to do, you were on a mobile phone, you were in Belgrade, and somebody else's client is phoning you. You're confused about what he is talking about. Then why would you give him an assurance that it doesn't matter, that it's not that urgent yet?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, my understanding, as I said, was that it is not a case now. I don't know in which capacity this person was acted or made some relations with my colleague. I was not aware about that. I mean, that's general information, not only to this person but to all persons that might call us at our office, because we collect many informations, and sometimes one of our witnesses will call maybe for our colleague Pisarevic. It's a normal way. I mean, it's a sensitive issue to deal with the witnesses or with someone who will get some information or whatever, so we always try to be very polite, very understandable, and not to be, you know, in some kind of, I would say, short conversation or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, why, if what you say is true, you didn't know really what that was all about, would you purport to give advice to another lawyer's client about something where there was a time issue? Why would you purport to give advice about -- when he says, "I thought it was going to be in" --

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: You know, the reason was simple. My guess was that maybe someone is interested what is the development in this case, or maybe he will act in capacity or he will appear in capacity of witness, or maybe in capacity of some other sort of person, so that the issue was, I mean, the general information, not only for this person but for all persons in our case, is that according to predicted schedule in this case, by the end of the year we could have our case here, I mean the Defence case. That was my general impression, and always I repeat that to all of our witnesses, the same thing. Like your team leader, Mrs. Inderhaug, she's in permanent contact with all your witnesses, arrange travels, see how they are doing. I mean, in spite of the unproportion between the Prosecutor and Defence, I mean in favour of Prosecutor, of course, with the sources and all those things, basically it's the same method.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you didn't think that Daki would be required as a witness until towards the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Actually, I wasn't aware at all about his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And yet you would give advice?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: In general terms, because I didn't know. Maybe he will give this information to a third person. Who knows? I mean, you cannot act, you know, so strictly on this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If you say so, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before re-examination, Mr. Pantelic, the question which Daki asked was, "When does that programme with Bane start?" Now, you say that you believe that was a reference to a witness protection programme. The witness protection programme with Bane, Bane being Mr. Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the last almost two years in this particular case, my colleagues and me, we are dealing permanent with this issue. A lot of witnesses ask, "How we can be protected? We are not Serb nationals. How we can come in The Hague to give our evidence, to give testimony?" In all our relations with them, we tried to explain the role of the Victim and Witness Unit here, I mean, in general terms. You cannot be specific so much with laypersons. So the same thing is with the Serb witnesses which we intend to call. They require a so-called safe passage issue, because they also have some, I would say, not fear but -- well, they have some reserves about their position because, frankly saying, they are a member of a local government there in the Samac area, et cetera, so it's understandable. So on many occasions, we have to speak with them. We have to convince them and to give some information such as. So, frankly, I wasn't able to make this slight difference, you know, at that moment. Maybe I was thinking that this person is asking for some other information about, you know, including this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A witness protection programme is --

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- because you cannot explain to them it's a unit. It's more familiar to them in our language to say, "Well, there is a protection programme," or something, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which is usually organised by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: By the Tribunal, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pantelic, just a point of clarification. You answered a question from Mr. Haynes, saying that you had been called on a mobile phone. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, how was it that Witness Agnes had the number of your mobile phone?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a very simple question. Actually, on many times we received the faxes from the Registry on our telephone for colleague Pisarevic and for many other colleagues in the Republika Srpska and in Belgrade too, so I mean it's a normal way of things. In terms of this telephone number, it's also usual for colleagues dealing with a joinder case, as we are dealing, to give, I would say, many telephones of all colleagues in case that someone wants to reach someone and he cannot be in contact, and then -- because you never know. Maybe some kind of very important information will come and a colleague is not here. Maybe the other can take this information and pass it to him. I'm dealing with this thing, I mean, all these years, and including with my colleague Pisarevic. If I have something to do in the Bosanski Samac area, I give to this person his number so he can call his office, leave a message or something. I mean, that's the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is customary for you to give the mobile number to potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: I didn't gave this telephone. You should ask, you know, the other persons. I didn't gave this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you didn't give the person your number?

utterances.speaker: IGOR PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... because I can't see this person, Mr. Agnes. I didn't have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have no re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, that concludes your evidence, and you are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I may, shall I just walk away or can I get my robe and to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you can resume your seat, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I call Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may address the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to suggest, for the hearing of my client Milan Simic, that the cross-examination be limited to general matters linked to this particular case and not to be expanded to questions that are not linked to this Rule 77 hearing. It is an irregular motion, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That will be the case. That has been the ruling. The questions have to be so limited. If they are not so limited, then an objection can be made and the Chamber will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your full name is Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: 9th of August, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you were married in 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could you just give us the date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The 1st of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones be moved up closer to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I married on the 1st of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We see that you're in a wheelchair. The event that caused you to be confined to a wheelchair, when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It took place on the 13th of February, 1993; that is, the 13th day into my marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you're a graduate in economics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated at the faculty of economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you ever been charged or convicted of any criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, never. I was never charged or convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you just one question about events in Bosanski Samac in 1992. Did you, in 1992, ever go to the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992 I went to the elementary school on one occasion, and that is what I told people from the Office of the Prosecutor, and this was also confirmed by Prosecutor witnesses that were interviewed by the Prosecutor subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, that's an interview at which, I think, Ms. Paterson was also present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you were in court when the witness we call Agnes was giving his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Had you ever seen that man before in your life?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, never. I've never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson or Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I'm to assume that I'm to be limited to those basically two questions, then my cross-examination is limited to that or do I have a certain amount of leeway beyond these couple of questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not so limited. You're entitled to deal with the subject matter of the application, but of course, as we have ruled, you cannot deal with questions which go to the guilt or innocence in the wider issue which we have not yet considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had no intention of going into those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we have met before, have we not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And as you said, we were together on the 2nd of March, 1998, when you gave a statement to the Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of March. I don't know the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And in that statement, as you've already said -- you admitted that you had been present at the primary school sometime in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I was in the elementary school. I didn't admit it. I just told you about events that occurred in 1992 linked to the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And at that same conversation, I asked you if -- I believe it came up in the discussions if there was someone that was known to you as your kum, which has been explained to me as your best man. Did we discuss someone, who was your best man, that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. You didn't ask me. I told you that he was my driver. He drove me to the elementary school and drove me back from the elementary school. So my kum was, at the same time, my driver in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: His name is Stevo Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, on the 23rd of June this year, a statement was submitted from your lawyer, in which you completely denied ever having met the person known as Mr. Agnes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you never, ever had a telephone conversation with Mr. Agnes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: You are right. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So you were here and heard the testimony of Mr. Agnes, and all those times that he said that he had meetings with you and all those times he said he had phone calls with you, none of that is correct; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. None of that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But you had heard about this person, Mr. Agnes, before you came to court for this proceeding, had you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard about very many people that my Defence counsel had contact with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, you, I assume, have regular conversations with your attorney, Mr. Avramovic, and discuss your defence and preparing for this case; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I ask Ms. Paterson treads a little carefully here. She is going into the area of attorney/client privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am simply asking did they have conversations. I have no intention of going into the substance of the conversations beyond the fact that they may, on occasion, have discussed Mr. Agnes. That's the extent of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Confine yourself in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did you, at any time in your conversations with Mr. Avramovic, discuss the fact that Mr. Agnes had volunteered to testify on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. That's a step too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're claiming the privilege on behalf of your client, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's only his to waive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So he's not prepared to waive it to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Don't you think it might be an idea to have some instructions on the point, because certain inferences can be drawn from --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- a refusal to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly. Perhaps he should be asked if he's happy to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Should I put the question to him, Your Honour, or do you want to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you have a right, if you want to, not to answer that question. Do you want to answer that question or not? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do want to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Please do so, then.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes. At any time during your conversations with Mr. Avramovic, when you were talking about preparing for your trial, did he ever mention to you the existence of this person known as Mr. Agnes, that this man had come forward and offered to testify for you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic did not tell me things to that effect, though I did discuss this with him. But when Mr. Agnes appeared as one of many that my attorney had contacted, my lawyer at the time was Mr. Vukovic. So I received the first information about Mr. Agnes from Mr. Vukovic and not Mr. Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. But the point is, you knew Mr. Agnes existed. You knew that this man had come forward and offered to give testimony favourable to you. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, what did you know about Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what Mr. Vukovic told me, I knew that he had contacted a man whom we call here Mr. Agnes, and he conveyed to me his impressions about this man very briefly, because, of course, we didn't discuss him only. We were having this conversation after my return from the spa in Igalo, so he was telling me about things that had happened in the meantime. Among other things, he told me, very briefly, with reference to Mr. Agnes, that his impressions as regards that individual were that he was a highly unreliable individual and that he would -- had still not decided whether he would be of any use for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you know a woman by the name of Jasna Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: That's a young woman who testified here in court earlier is week; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And Ms. Marosevic is a personal friend of yours, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And she's been trying to assist you in your preparation to your defence for this case, has she not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a sense. Up to a point. Not directly to assist the Defence, because she is not qualified to assist, but she did tell me that she had contacted a friend of hers that she thought might be useful for my defence, and I told her then the telephone number of my lawyer, Mr. Vukovic, that she should contact him and tell him everything that she knew, and that it was then up to him to decide what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Did Jasna ever tell you that she was a friend of Mr. Agnes, that she had known him before the war started?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: She told me that this friend of hers that she thought might be useful, that she did know that person from before the war and that she was a friend of his, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And did you ever have any more detailed discussions with her about Mr. Agnes, about the fact that he had volunteered to testify on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any detailed discussion with her about anything linked to my defence at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Didn't you find it rather curious, Mr. Simic, that a man that you claim you've never met before and you've never seen before in your life was willing to come forward and testify on your behalf in a trial as serious as this here in The Hague? Did that surprise you that Mr. Agnes volunteered to testify for you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: First of all, if we're talking about my conversation with Jasna, all she told me was that he was willing to talk to my attorney. Whether this was a question of testimony or something else, I didn't know. Secondly, it does not surprise me at all if people want to appear in this court to tell the truth. He's not supposed to testify for or against me but to testify of things that he witnessed and tell the Court what he saw. I don't see how the Court would operate at all if people weren't ready to come here and tell the Court what they know. So I'm not surprised at all. And surely other witnesses come on the basis of that same principle, to tell the Court what they know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, up until, I guess it was late May or early -- I guess sometime in June of this year, you were actually on what's called provisional release and you were living in Bosanski Samac; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So unlike the other defendants in this case who are in the detention centre, you've been in Bosanski Samac and you've been free to move around and meet people and have conversations, go out to cafes, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And one of the cafes that you hang out at, that you go to frequently, is the cafe Lotos, where Jasna is a waitress; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: You don't go to the cafe Lotos ever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not frequently. You said whether I hang out there and whether I go there frequently. I'm saying that I don't. I don't hang out there and I don't go there frequently. Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, you heard both Mr. Agnes and Jasna say that on several occasions Mr. Agnes went to Bosanski Samac in 1998 and 1999. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that most people in Bosanski Samac know who you are because of the unfortunate fact that you're in a wheelchair? You're well known around town because of your being confined to a wheelchair; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most people know me because of two unfortunate facts. One is that I'm in a wheelchair, and the other is that you have accused me. That is the other fact by which I'm known.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So is it your testimony, Mr. Simic, that never, in all those months of 1998 and 1999, and all those trips that Mr. Agnes went to Bosanski Samac, the two of you never crossed paths? You never crossed on the street? You never met in a cafe? You never laid eyes on each other? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that I never saw him or never identified him. I may have come across him in the street. I may have met you in the street sometime before the war, but I don't recollect that. I don't know all the people I come across in the street. It is possible that I may have come across him but I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, you've been here throughout all of the testimony. You heard all of Mr. Agnes's testimony, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I have read all his statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, if you've read his statements and you've heard his testimony, you know that he describes several meetings in which he claims to have met you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I know that in his first statement he said he never saw or heard me. Then in the second one he said he heard me on the phone. Then in the latest one he said he saw me several times. So my expectation was that at the end we saw each other on a daily basis. So he says all kinds of things in those statements, so I don't know which one of those you want me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I'll get back to that in just a minute. You, in the past, have worked at several different jobs, have you not, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Actually, I was mostly doing the same work but at different places.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you ever work for a company or work at a company called Nova Forma?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It depends what exactly you mean. My company, my firm, is called Osvit, and it did work for a firm called Nova Forma, as it did for other firms in Samac. I printed paper for them, publicity material, and so on. So my firm did work for that firm. So we have a business relationship, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So is it, then, just a complete coincidence that Mr. Agnes mentioned the fact that on at least one occasion you had a meeting with him at the Nova Forma company?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agnes, according to what he said here, doesn't even know where the premises of Nova Forma are situated. Of course, that is not true, as everything else that Mr. Agnes has said is not true. I was never in Nova Forma with Mr. Agnes and, anyway, I went to Nova Forma only once. When they were observing their first anniversary, I went there. I was one of the invited guests to that modest celebration. And it is very complicated for me to reach Nova Forma, because you have to reach it from the main road and not from town. So you need to go through a different gate than the gate leading to Buducnost.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So then, Mr. Simic, in all the places in Bosanski Samac that Mr. Agnes could have picked to claim that he met you, it's just an amazing coincidence that he picked the Nova Forma company with which you, in fact, do have a business association; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: What I am saying is that I have business relations with all firms in Samac. There isn't a firm with which my printing firm does not have business relations; some to a greater, others to a lesser extent. That is my market. My printing office is not a big one to cover a broader area beyond Samac. So if you mention any firm in Samac, they would be my business partners. The fact that he chose Nova Forma, that depended on his own sources of information, which were mostly rumours and gossip. I have another link to Nova Forma, and that is that I was president of the board of managers of the state-owned company Buduchnost, and then Buduchnost rented out a part of the premises to Marijan Misic, who set up a company called Nova Forma. So I was on the other side. I was working in the state-owned company, which rented out the premises to the owner of Nova Forma. So he may have linked those up two. And the owner of Nova Forma is Marijan Misic, who is my friend and who had worked with me in Buduchnost before the war. He was technical director and I was financial director. So we know each other very well. As for who is the owner of Nova Forma, that is easy to check in court where the firm has been registered. It can't be simply based on what Agnes says or what you claim, but there are documents to corroborate and to show who owns the company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you heard the testimony that Mr. Agnes is not originally from Bosanski Samac, that he's from -- was originally from the town of Bihac in Bosnia. Did you hear that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you also heard the testimony that on the 17th of April, Mr. Agnes was arrested and then detained in the camps until December, when he joined the VRS army, and stayed in the VRS army until October, when he went to Serbia. You heard that testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard the testimony, but I don't recall all the dates. But I did hear the testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So what you're trying to tell us is that Mr. Agnes, who was not even from Bosanski Samac, didn't spend much time in Bosanski Samac, went to all the trouble to apparently investigate who owned the Nova Forma company, that there might be a connection between you and the Buducnost company, and that maybe that was a good place he could choose to say, untruthfully, that he had had a meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't investigate things properly, as far as I remember his testimony. Perhaps I'm wrong, but he didn't convey a single exact fact regarding the ownership of Nova Forma. Who he got his information from, I have no idea; nor am I interested; nor do I wish to investigate how he gets his information. But they are obviously wrong. This is something that you yourself can easily see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you ever have an office with your printing company or any of your other business interests in the building called the Spomen Dom, which I believe is also known as the Memorial Centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And you also heard Mr. Agnes say that he had a meeting with you in the Spomen Dom, in your office there on one occasion, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: When, when? When did we meet there in Spomen Dom?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I have that exact reference in front of me, but do you remember Mr. Agnes testifying here that he met with you at least once in the Spomen Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember that he testified to that effect here, but unfortunately at the time my office was not in the Spomen Dom. So the period that he states that he met me in Spomen Dom, my office wasn't in Spomen Dom at all, so I couldn't have met him there. He did not meet me there; anywhere or there either. If you can check it out, do so and tell me when it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Do you have a relative -- I don't know whether it's a close or distant relative -- by the name Simeun Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Simeun Simic, yes, I have. He's a close relative. It is my cousin, my uncle's child.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Does he also maintain some offices in the Spomen Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: He is the director of a state company called Duga, and their premises are in Spomen Dom. So he's the director of that company within the composition of which is the Memorial Centre building, the Spomen Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So again, Mr. Simic, apparently we're left to just assume that it's an amazing coincidence that Mr. Agnes came in and said that he met with you in the Spomen Dom, where you used to have an office and where a close relative of yours still has an office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what that's got to do with where my relative works and where his office is. I have an office there too today because I returned to the Spomen Dom. But unfortunately, as I've already said, Mr. Agnes and you said, to begin with, that people know me in Samac because of one unfortunate incident, and I said because of two unfortunate incidents, so people do have information about me and it's no problem to learn where my printing press outfit is located, because I have a lot of advertising material. And the unfortunate fact for Mr. Agnes is that this office moved to the Duga and then back to the Spomen Dom, so that he couldn't know exactly when the printing company was where, and he mixed up the dates and he mixed up the premises. He doesn't know. But I know when I was situated in the office which was in the Buducnost building and when I was at my office situated in the Spomen Dom building, and Mr. Agnes simply did not know that and he mixed up the dates. So when I was in the Buducnost premises, he said he saw me in the Spomen Dom. When I was in the Spomen Dom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you're creating some hardship for the interpreters. Could you speak a little slower.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I shall try, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour, for drawing my attention to that. Well, that's my answer. I've answered it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: No, I think that you just mentioned that you have now returned to the Spomen Dom, that you now again have offices in the Spomen Dom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And when did you return to the Spomen Dom, take offices again in that building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: At the end of March or the beginning of April this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, end of April, beginning of March -- or end of March, beginning of April; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I said somewhere towards the end of March or the beginning of April. That's what I think, although I have it in my notes, in my documents, when I -- one contract ceased to exist and when I signed another contact, so I'm not sure whether it was at the end of March or the beginning of April. But, of course, if you want the exact date, I can get it for you, looking back in my documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Simic, Mr. Agnes came to the attention of the Tribunal in early May of 1999, this year, so from what you're saying, you again had offices in the Spomen Dom before Mr. Agnes left Bosanski Samac and came and told the Tribunal his allegations against you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I said when I was in the Spomen Dom again, and that's got nothing to do with where Mr. Agnes was. I don't know where he was, and I don't know when he was where. I know when I moved from the Buducnost building to the Spomen Dom, and I see no connection with where he was, with anything to do with where he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Simic, I know you said that you were getting rehabilitation in Montenegro, I believe, during the month of August 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And I believe in September that you were here at The Hague for a few days for another court proceeding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But considering the months of October, November and December, 1998, during those months were you in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And in 1999, were you in Bosanski Samac in January, February and March?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course. Where else would I be?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So while I know that you deny that you ever met with Mr. Agnes, in fact you were in Bosanski Samac during that six-month period when he claims to have had several meetings with you; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It is true that I was in Bosanski Samac, because that is what this Tribunal told me to do, and I complied and did not leave Bosanski Samac in conformity with the ruling made by this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, that concludes your testimony. You are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, where are you now in your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I now have to move into evidence a file of documents. I have a copy for each of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And one for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The Prosecution have had one for some days now, I think. If I may just take you through it briefly, the first section is the entire documentary evidence filed by the Defence during the course of these proceedings. You'll see there's an index on the second page which describes the document, gives the page numbers of the document in both Serbian and in English, and in the third column the date on which it was filed. The second section I need to take you to is headed "Admitted Facts." Now, I've spoken to Mr. Ryneveld about this, and the Prosecution have considered their position so far as this is concerned. Most of these facts were served on all parties, I think, as long as three months ago, with a requirement that they comment upon it, and, perhaps predictably, the only response is from Mr. Brashich. But the Prosecution position, as I understand it, is that they cannot admit all of those as facts. They are happy that the first four are admitted as facts, and they are content that the documents in Section 1 purport to establish each of those facts. So rather than it being headed "Admitted Facts," it probably ought to be headed "Statement of Facts," and I hope that's not controversial.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: That's a relatively accurate description of our understanding. Our point was simply on this Section 2 that's entitled "Admitted Facts," we absolutely have no problem with numbers 1 to 4, but numbers 5 to 11, which basically describe what is in the documents that are listed in Section 1, we are not in a position to confirm whether those things are true or not. We have no way of verifying that information, so we can't admit them as facts. But we have no objection to the documents being admitted, and the documents can speak for themselves and Your Honours can give them whatever weight you see fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand the title is changed from "Admitted Facts" to "Statement of Facts"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it would normally be my practice to read that document so that it appears on the transcript of evidence. I would be grateful for some guidance as to the practice in relation to such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That won't be necessary. You're putting it in, you're exhibiting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, which brings us to Section 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before you do, I'm sorry to come back to it, but it does not contain the interview which Mr. Simic had in which he said that he had been at the elementary school. I thought you were going to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm endeavouring to. I obtained a copy of that interview last night, and I have it here. But I obtained it from Defence counsel in the main case, who has heavily marked the relevant passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There must be a copy available from the Prosecution, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I hope we can sort that out before I close my case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If you are going to give us time at the break, I can go to my computer and print out a fresh copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that this copy should be redacted only to the passage which contains his admission that he was at the elementary school on one occasion, and not the whole statement of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is how it should be done. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just so I can be clear, Your Honours, basically the way the interview was conducted was that Mr. Simic was given an opportunity, without any interruptions, to tell us whatever he wanted to tell us about what had happened, and it goes on for approximately four pages in the transcript, and I believe the first reference to the elementary school is on the top of the third page of this part of his testimony, where he states, and I'm just going to read one sentence, quite simply: "So we went to the elementary school between 11.00 at night and midnight." Is that sufficient for Court purposes, to just have that one sentence, or should I give you the whole four pages of his statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suggest that you speak to Mr. Haynes about it. If he wants some more in, then you may like to consider including it. But we certainly don't want anything other than anything which explains its context.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Haynes and I can work that out at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't want to go to the wider issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which brings us to Section 3 of the bundle of documents and the vexed question of affidavit evidence. Now, I do submit that even under the old Rule, the evidence of Spasoje Pisarevic is in a form that is admissible before this Tribunal. Just so it is clear, the witness statement is signed in the form of a declaration admissible under Serbian law as a declaration, and to double up, as it were, to add the belt to the braces, it is postulated under The Hague Convention of 1933. Now, I know I don't need to address Your Honours at any length about the absence of an affidavit, as we in common-law countries understand it to be, from the Yugoslavian legal system, but they do have a system of declarations -- I see Ms. Paterson rising.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can speed things up, Your Honour. I believe that we stated yesterday unequivocally we have no objection to introducing this document. Please submit it into evidence. We're happy to have Your Honours consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I was only concerned that, notwithstanding concessions yesterday, the Court had, on an earlier occasion, indicated that the document was not in an appropriate form. If it now is, then I do submit that into evidence, along with all the other documents that the Defence rely upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The concession is not that it's in an appropriate form. The concession is that you may tender it. That's all we need to worry about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm concerned that the Court should receive it as admissible evidence, not just as some document that has no status at all. Very well. Then subject to the interview, that is all the evidence that the Defence propose to call in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just before we leave this matter of documents, I just want to clarify. We also have another bright orange binder, which is the binders Mr. Haynes has been using. It contains all of Mr. Agnes' witness statements that were, I believe, tendered as Defence exhibits. I would just like to clarify. Have those been entered into evidence? We would like that they be entered into evidence, so if they have not, we would like to be sure they do go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We did make a ruling that they should be admitted into evidence. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All the statements, the Prosecution statements of Witness Agnes, are admitted into evidence, and they will be put on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to clarify that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There is, of course, one other thing of actually great importance, and that is the re-revised transcript of a telephone conversation which ought to now become, I submit, Exhibit 1A, and all other copies should be removed from the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would form part of the evidence and would be an exhibit, but it wouldn't displace those that had been submitted before, tendered before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I am concerned about this because I've seen the report from the translation service, and it's significant because the effect of it is that the most crucial line in the telephone conversation between Mr. Agnes and Mr. Avramovic is now said to be unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but the point is really this: That therefore means that the original Exhibit 1A is an erroneous translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a matter for us to look at and to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we did have a deal of debate about this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's why it should be in evidence. What weight we give to the first one is a matter for us, but you may rest assured that if the translation people say they can no longer decide between one and the other, that may very well be the attitude we take. I'm not going to bind anybody to that, but it seems to be the common-sense one. But to exclude an exhibit about which there has been a lot of debate in the evidence seems to me, with respect, to be absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it really depends whether, in requiring a further translation, you were looking for a definitive answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are not a jury, so let's get on with it. I do submit, therefore, that the new translation should become Exhibit 1C, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Registrar will see to that. Is that your case now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, subject to the passage of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll now move to the stage of addresses, beginning with the Prosecution. Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the termination of the giving of evidence, I was wondering, rather than my disrupting the proceedings thereafter, I would beg leave to be released, inasmuch as I have to be in court tomorrow in New York. I believe Mr. Pantelic is in the same predicament as I am. And I would again beg leave of the Court, since I have no further role, that I be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, yes, you may be released. I should say that the other matter in which you are involved, obviously we will not reach it and you will be advised as to the future dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make it clear that I had also spoken on behalf of Mr. Pantelic, so that we not speak twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic also may be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In fact, all counsel that wish to leave, other than those who are intimately involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to inform the Court, I appreciate the fact that Your Honours are anxious to conclude the case today. I will endeavour to keep that in mind. I just want to advise you that I have read through my summation on a couple of occasions, and I estimate it does run about an hour. I will try to shorten it as much as possible, but just so you know for scheduling purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may also submit a written form.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour, but my submission is written in outline form, so we're not prepared to submit anything that formal. If you bear with me, I'll just go ahead and give it and I'll try and be concise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issue before you is whether or not Mr. Avramovic and Mr. Simic threatened, intimidated, caused any injury to, offered a bribe to, or otherwise interfered with a potential witness, specifically the man referred to as Mr. Agnes, before this Trial Chamber. By its very nature, this crime is committed behind closed doors, with few witnesses. Therefore, for the most part, this case is going to hinge on the credibility of the three key witnesses in this case, that being Mr. Agnes, Mr. Avramovic, and Mr. Simic. So in making your determination in this case, it's crucial that you pay attention to the credibility of those witnesses and particularly to their motivation in coming before you and giving the testimony that they did. Now, if someone were to come in and start to listen to this case in the middle of the testimony, they might think this was a fairly complicated case. They would have heard about a lot of different meetings on different dates, different occasions, different people that were present. But Your Honours have been here and have been listening to the testimony, and you know that this, in fact, is not that terribly complicated a case. What it boils down to, quite simply, is the word of Mr. Agnes against the word of Mr. Avramovic and Mr. Simic. Yes, there were other witnesses called, but those were the three key witnesses in this case. I know there are many ways to evaluate a witness's credibility, and I'm sure that each of you have your own tried and true tested ways, but I would stress that in this particular case, I think the motivation in coming forward and giving the testimony that they gave is especially important. We must ask ourselves: What did Mr. Agnes have to gain or lose by coming in and telling the Court the story that he did? On the other hand, what motivation did Mr. Avramovic have to give his version of events? Finally, what motivation did Mr. Simic have to give his testimony? Finally, the ultimate question that Your Honours have to decide is: Did Mr. Agnes volunteer to give testimony on behalf of Milan Simic, or was he forced or were they attempting to force him to give testimony on Mr. Simic's behalf? Let's begin with Mr. Agnes. Your Honours saw him come in and give testimony over several days. You are aware of the fact that he has been here in The Hague since May as a protected witness. He did not testify until November. He was here almost eight months waiting to give his testimony. You heard him state that he left behind his family in Serbia. He took it upon himself to leave and come to the attention of the Tribunal by going to SFOR in Brcko. And you heard him say that he was afraid to come forward, that he was greatly concerned for his security and that of his family. That was corroborated by the testimony of our investigator, Tore Soldal. He told that he met Mr. Agnes the day he had turned himself into SFOR and that, in his opinion, Mr. Agnes was afraid. Mr. Soldal told you that, despite his fears, the only thing that Mr. Agnes asked from the Tribunal was for security. He did not ask for a job. He did not ask for money. He did not ask, even at that point, to be resettled to another country. Ultimately, when we brought him here and put him in protection, it was agreed he would be resettled to another country, but that is the only thing he has ever asked for and the only thing he has ever been promised. All he really wanted was to be safe and for his family to be safe. What was his motivation in coming forward? His motivation was to take control of his life back. Now, we know why he came forward. Let's look at the story he told. Now, I will admit that Mr. Agnes was far from the perfect witness. There were times when he was somewhat difficult, when he was frustrated and angry, but in many ways that makes him a very credible witness. You saw him come in here. You saw for yourselves his emotions. He did not keep his emotions to himself. You saw when he got angry, you saw when he got frustrated, and you saw when he got outraged at some of the allegations being made against him by the Defence. Now, from the very beginning he's admitted some things about himself that were not necessarily terribly positive. Mr. Soldal told you that in their very first interview, Mr. Agnes admitted this unfortunate incident where Mr. Agnes was accused of accidentally discharging a gun, and a young girl was shot, while he was in the army. He admitted that, as a Muslim, he had joined the army of the Republika Srpska and served for several months in that army. He admitted to Mr. Soldal that he used a different name when he was in Serbia. He also, when confronted with the infamous blue bag, admitted that that was his. He didn't attempt to deny that. He also admitted that he had left certain things out of his statements. He acknowledged that he gave several statements to the Tribunal and that with each successive statement, he gave some more details, but he explained why he did that. Again, it was because he was afraid. He was waiting to see if the Tribunal could give him the security he wanted. Once he started to feel comfortable with his protection, he gave more and more information, including the fact that he had met Milan Simic. And if Your Honours look at the statement, you will see what he was concerned about: protecting not only himself and his family but his friends and acquaintances in Bosanski Samac. And if you read his early statement, you will see that he even went so far as to try and protect Jasna Marosevic and her father. And as you know, Jasna came and testified for the Defence, but he tried to keep her out of these events as much as he could. Now, you will remember in his cross-examination that Mr. Haynes challenged many of the things that Mr. Agnes has said and done, and tried to allude to the fact that these were all bad things that he had done and that he was willing to do anything to save himself when he was afraid. But what is wrong with some of the things that he did? If you think about it, almost anyone would do what he did in his situation. Mr. Haynes would like you to believe that it was a terrible thing that Mr. Agnes may have left Serbia -- one of the reasons he may have left Serbia was to avoid being mobilised into the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and being sent to fight in Kosovo, but, of course, hundreds, if not thousands, of young men left Serbia to avoid being mobilised and fighting in Kosovo. Mr. Agnes did his time in the army, he did his time in the detention camps in Bosnia, and he had no desire whatsoever to be in any army ever again. Yes, Mr. Agnes changed his name. Whether he did it legally or not, what difference does it make? He did it for very practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: He was a Muslim living in Serbia, and, as his uncle said, it would be easier for him on a daily basis if he took a Serbian name. It's a very practical solution under the circumstances. Mr. Haynes also alluded to the fact that from the day he joined the VRS, Mr. Agnes wanted nothing more than to get out of the army. Of course he did. He didn't want to join the army in the first place. The only reason he joined the army was to get out of forced labour, to get out of the detention camps that he was in, and he was looking for an opportunity to get out. Now, Mr. Agnes did discuss some questionable things. The question arises about his testimony concerning his uncle and whether or not his uncle paid some money to get him out of the VRS. Now, Mr. Agnes, in his statement, did tell Tore Soldal that his uncle gave some money to someone that he thinks led to his getting out of the army. When he came in to testify, he was reluctant to admit that. But I submit, Your Honours, that he was reluctant to admit that because Mr. Haynes was fashioning that as a crime of bribery. He was asking Mr. Agnes to say that his uncle, who was acting out of concern for Mr. Agnes, had committed a crime in order to him to get out of the army. He did not want to characterise that as bribery, but he did admit that his uncle did what he could to assist him and perhaps even to get him out of the army. Mr. Haynes has also alluded to the fact that perhaps Mr. Agnes is a wanted criminal; that he's here as a fugitive from justice; that he's been indicted for murder and has fled from the prosecution. But I contend, Your Honours, if that were the fact, the Defence or the, in fact, government of Republika Srpska would have brought to your attention the fact that there was an outstanding warrant for Mr. Agnes's arrest, and to my knowledge that has not been done. Then there's the issue of the military ID card that we spent so much time on. There's no need to go over that again. Your Honours heard that testimony in great detail. Mr. Agnes vehemently denied that that was his document. It clearly is a tampered-with document, if not an outright forged document, and we contend that Mr. Agnes's testimony should be believed, that that was not his document and that he never saw it before. Now, many of the things that the Defence is trying to argue in some way incriminate Mr. Agnes just don't make any sense when you stop and think about it. The Defence has made a big issue about this infamous blue bag, this bag that, according to the Defence, was left at Jasna's house, and, according to Mr. Agnes, was left with his friend in Brcko. But as we've said, stop and think about the circumstances. Mr. Agnes said that he was planning to leave. According to him, he was being put under pressure to testify. He wanted nothing more to do with it. He wanted to somehow get to the Tribunal and bring this to our attention. Needless to say, he didn't want Jasna to know his plans. He didn't want Mr. Simic or Mr. Avramovic to know. What he wanted to do was try and slip away and stay away as long as possible before anyone noticed. Now, if you were going to do that, would you leave your bag at the home of Jasna or would you leave it with a friend? I contend you would leave it with your friend, not with Jasna. And if, in fact, you were trying to leave and not be traced and not have people find out that you had left, would you leave your identification card in the bag? Why not throw it in the river? Why not burn it? Why not bury it under a rock? There are many different ways he could have gotten rid of that ID card. It makes no sense whatsoever that he would have left the card and the bag with Jasna. And he gave you a logical explanation. He left the bag with a friend in Brcko and he went to SFOR. He thought, if he took the bag with all his belongings, that it might be suspicious. What he might have been thinking is, "Well, I don't know, when I go to SFOR, if they're going to take me. I don't know if the Tribunal is going to talk to me. If they kick me out and tell me to go home, at least I can go back to my friend's house in Brcko, pick up my belongings, and go my own way." If he left the bag at Jasna's, was he really going to go to SFOR, risk that they would not let him in and then have to go back to Jasna's and explain where he had been and perhaps have her become suspicious? I contend that none of that makes any sense, Your Honours, and the only version of the blue bag that makes sense is that of Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, we'll have to take the break at four, so when you come to a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try and get through the section on Mr. Agnes. It shouldn't take much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not too fast, though. They are complaining about the speed of your address.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I know this is a problem that I have, but I'm from New York, and we speak fast in New York. When you think about the story that Mr. Agnes told, and of course we contend that it wasn't a story but the truth, we have a saying in my country that the Devil is in the details. And I think everyone knows, if you're going to tell a lie, it's always easier to keep it short and simple. And I contend that it's the details that, in fact, are what corroborate Mr. Agnes's testimony. If he was going to make up this entire story, if none of this is true, why would he tell so many details? Why not just say there was one meeting at which the pressure was put on him? Just say there was one meeting when the money and the job and the apartment were offered? Why say that there were several meetings at several different locations, that many different people were present? Why go to the trouble to say that it was at the Nova Forma company, one of the meetings, and that another meeting was at Spomen Dom, if that didn't really happen? By giving that much detail, he was only forcing himself to have to repeat that over and over and over again. And I contend that if you compare the statements that he gave to the Tribunal with his testimony here before you, you will find that in the majority of cases the testimony is consistent. Remember some of the details that he gave. For almost every meeting he described, he had something in particular he could remember. Either it was where the meeting took place, it was when the meeting took place, it was who was present, or in some cases it was things like the documents that were shown to him. Remember when he talked about the last meeting in Bosanski Samac when this man Spasoje Pisarevic appeared. Remember how he talked about how Mr. Pisarevic brought out these lists of names. He asked Mr. Agnes to tell him everything he knew about these names. Mr. Agnes said, "I couldn't tell him. I only knew their nicknames. So Mr. Pisarevic volunteered the information. And then we went become to the house where Mr. Pisarevic had an office." Why would he make up these details? How could he make up these details unless these conversations had actually happened, unless and he had actually been to these locations? And what about his allegation about the witness preparation session? This was confirmed, Your Honours, by the audio tape. Mr. Agnes told you the very interesting detail, that Mr. Avramovic had told him that sometime in May he would have to go to Bosanski Samac where he would be put through what was called a witness preparation session. They would go over his testimony. And as Your Honours know, we played the audio tape. It was their quite clearly on the tape, the conversation with Mr. Pantelic, about the programme. You heard Mr. Pantelic's explanation of the programme, and I leave if to Your Honours to decide whether you believe his explanation or not. I contend that his explanation is incredibly far-fetched, that Mr. Agnes's is the one that you should believe, and that's just one more detail that corroborates the testimony ever Mr. Agnes. Remember too that Mr. Agnes did not over-exaggerate his testimony. On one of the really key questions put to him -- I believe by you, Judge Bennouna -- you asked Mr. Agnes: "Did Mr. Avramovic ever threaten you to your face? Did he ever threaten to harm you? Did he ever threaten to harm your family?" And what did he say? "No." How much more compelling would his testimony have been, how much more dramatic would it have been to say, "Yes. He threatened me to my face"? But he didn't. He didn't want to lie he wanted to tell you the truth. He said, "No. The threats were more subtle than. It was anonymous phone calls. It was people coming by the house. It was gunshots. It was not a threat to my face. No, Mr. Avramovic didn't do that, and, no, Mr. Simic didn't do that either." He did not exaggerate. He told you the truth. It's our contention, Your Honour, at that Mr. Agnes kept his promise to you. He came here, he promised to tell you the truth. He stayed here eight months by himself under very lonely conditions waiting to testify. It was not an easy time for Mr. Agnes. You saw him come in, you saw him come back day after day. He submitted to a grilling cross-examination. You saw his emotions out there on his sleeve, and I contend, Your Honours, that that all goes to his credibility. As I said, he's done his part, he's kept his promise, and now he just wants his life back. I think, Your Honours, that perhaps is a good point to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, I've been requested to ask you to speak a little slower, notwithstanding your place of origin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best. Now I would like to turn to the testimony of Mr. Neskovic. As you know, Mr. Neskovic's testimony was brief, but it was significant in its own way. Mr. Neskovic did confirm some things and did corroborate some things Mr. Agnes said. He confirmed that, in fact, there was the meeting at Mr. Agnes's house in late September in Sremska Mitrovica. Mr. Neskovic admitted he was not present when Mr. Avramovic spoke with Mr. Agnes, so he was not in a position to know what the substance of that conversation was about, and Mr. Neskovic did say that when he went into the dining room to find out how long they were going to be, he did notice files spread around and he could hear them briefly speaking about events in Bosanski Samac in 1992. All of that is consistent with what Mr. Agnes said went on. I think the one thing that's most troubling about Mr. Neskovic's testimony is that, like Mr. Vukovic, he wants us to believe that he had no interest in Mr. Agnes either. Mr. Neskovic said that the day before they went to this meeting, he had been retained to defend Mr. Todorovic. Mr. Neskovic was the deputy minister of justice for the Republika Srpska, was familiar with the indictment against Mr. Todorovic, and knew that among the charges against Mr. Todorovic were some that allegedly occurred in the camps in Bosanski Samac. Here he was sitting in a house with a man who was detained in one of those camps, who, according to the Defence, was willing to cooperate with the Defence, and Mr. Neskovic would like us to believe that he had absolutely no interest whatsoever in talking to Mr. Agnes and asking him a few questions about his client. I contend, Your Honours, that that is a highly improbable sequence of events. Now let's discuss the testimony of Mr. Vukovic. Mr. Vukovic's testimony was also short, but again he confirmed and corroborated some of the things that Mr. Agnes said. As you will recall, he confirmed that there were at least two meetings that he had with Mr. Agnes, although they disagree on when and where those meetings took place. Mr. Vukovic did confirm that there was at least one meeting at the Jetset Cafe in Bosanski Samac. And again, most damning about the testimony of Mr. Vukovic was his description of how he handled the case for defending Mr. Simic. Again, Mr. Vukovic insists that Mr. Agnes was of no value to him whatsoever as a witness. Here is a witness who has come forward, if you believe the Defence version of the facts, and volunteered to testify for the Defence. Mr. Agnes was willing to say, first of all, that he never even saw Milan Simic in the primary school, and at the very least, even if Mr. Simic was in the primary school, Mr. Agnes never saw him lay a hand on anyone and never saw him harm anyone. But Mr. Vukovic wants us to believe that this is a witness who was absolutely of no significance to him and that he immediately found him to be not credible. As a result of that, Mr. Vukovic threw away all of his notes that he had made about his conversations with Mr. Agnes and conveniently apparently for the Tribunal, he decided not to bill for that meeting either. I contend, Your Honours, that this is a highly improbable sequence of events and puts all of the testimony of Mr. Vukovic in question. Now let's go to the other witness for the Prosecution, Mr. Mirsad Sahanic. As you will recall, Mr. Sahanic was a friend of Mr. Agnes. He was a policeman who happened to be assigned to Bosanski Samac in April of 1992. Unfortunately for Mr. Sahanic, he was in Bosanski Samac the day it was attacked and the war started, and, along with Mr. Agnes, he was arrested and detained for several months in the camps there. You learned that Mr. Sahanic is a married man, has a family, has a job, is living his own life, minding his own business, when, out of the blue, sometime back in 1998, he starts to get some phone calls from Jasna Marosevic and Mr. Agnes. None of those three witnesses dispute the fact that there were phone calls between Jasna and Mirsad and between Mr. Agnes and Mirsad. The Defence would like you to believe that none of the meetings took place or that other things happened at the meetings, but they cannot dispute the fact that there were phone calls between Jasna and Mirsad and between Mr. Agnes and Mirsad.
